title: 5. The modern data stack (cloud ELT)
summary: Managed ELT connectors into a cloud warehouse such as Snowflake, transformed with dbt and served through BI and reverse ETL: why it won, what it costs at scale, and how vendor sprawl creeps in.

blocks.text: The fifth reference architecture is the one many readers already work in. The 'modern data stack' (MDS) took the enterprise warehouse's ideas (chapter 37), moved them onto elastic cloud warehouses, swapped ETL for ELT, and assembled the platform from managed SaaS products. It became dominant roughly between 2016 and 2022 and is still the default for small and mid-sized analytics teams.
41.1 Context and the problem it solved

Three changes made it possible. Cloud warehouses (Redshift in 2012, then Snowflake and BigQuery) separated storage from compute and billed by use, so transformation inside the warehouse became cheap and elastic (chapter 26). Managed connectors made extraction from SaaS APIs a configuration task instead of a project. dbt made SQL transformations versioned, tested and modular, applying software engineering practice to analytics work (chapter 31).

ELT does not mean 'no modelling'. It means the transformation runs *after* loading, inside the warehouse, as SQL. The dimensional modelling of chapter 8 and the layering of chapter 12 apply unchanged.
41.2 Reference diagram

blocks.title: Modern data stack
blocks.caption: Everything converges on the warehouse. Reverse ETL sends modelled data back out to operational tools.

blocks.text: Connectors replicate source tables and API objects into **raw schemas** in the warehouse, typically one schema per source, with incremental syncs every 5 minutes to 24 hours. dbt models read raw tables through `source()` references and build **staging** models (rename, cast, deduplicate), **intermediate** models (joins and business logic) and **marts** (facts and dimensions for consumers). BI tools query the marts, ideally through a semantic layer. **Reverse ETL** reads modelled tables such as `customer_360` and pushes fields into Salesforce, HubSpot or ad platforms.
41.3 Components and technology choices

head: Layer
Component
Typical tools
rows: Fivetran, Airbyte, Stitch, dlt, Snowflake connectors, Snowpipe
SQL models with tests and lineage
dbt Core or dbt Cloud, SQLMesh
dbt Cloud jobs, Airflow, Dagster, Prefect
dbt tests, Elementary, Monte Carlo, Soda
Looker, Power BI, Tableau, dbt Semantic Layer, Cube

blocks.text: **Where Iceberg, Snowflake and semantic models fit.** Snowflake is the reference warehouse here and the centre of gravity of the whole stack. Iceberg was originally absent: data lived in Snowflake's internal format. Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables now let the same dbt models write open-format tables that other engines can read, which is the main bridge from MDS to the open lakehouse (chapters 28 and 42). Semantic models are first-class in the MDS, but frequently duplicated across several BI tools, which is exactly the problem chapter 35 addresses.
41.4 Modelling and data layers in this architecture

head: dbt layer
Medallion equivalent

rows: Tables written by connectors; never modified by dbt
One model per source table: rename, cast, dedupe; usually views

blocks.title: Incremental fact model in dbt on Snowflake
blocks.text:
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='order_id',
    incremental_strategy='merge',
    cluster_by=['order_date']
) }}

select
    o.order_id,
    o.customer_id,
    o.order_date,
    o.status,
    o.amount_usd,
    o._fivetran_synced as loaded_at
from {{ ref('stg_shop__orders') }} o
{% if is_incremental() %}
where o._fivetran_synced > (select max(loaded_at) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}

Note the incremental filter uses the connector's sync timestamp, not the business date, so late-arriving updates to old orders are still picked up. Connectors add such metadata columns (`_fivetran_synced`, `_fivetran_deleted`, or `_airbyte_extracted_at` for Airbyte); check the current naming for your connector version.

blocks.title: Source freshness and tests (dbt)
blocks.text:
version: 2
sources:
  - name: shop
    database: raw
    schema: shopify
    loaded_at_field: _fivetran_synced
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 24, period: hour}
    tables:
      - name: orders
        columns:
          - name: id
            tests:
              - unique
              - not_null
41.5 Ingestion, orchestration and serving

Ingestion is configured, not coded: choose a connector, authorise it, pick tables, set a sync frequency. Database sources typically use log-based CDC under the hood (chapter 17); SaaS sources use API polling with cursors. Files and events land through Snowpipe or Snowpipe Streaming. The trade-off is control: when a connector handles a schema change badly or an API changes, the team waits for the vendor.

Orchestration is often minimal at first: connectors sync on their own schedule and dbt runs on a cron in dbt Cloud. That breaks when dbt runs before a sync finishes. Mature setups use an orchestrator (Dagster, Airflow) that triggers dbt after connector syncs complete, or that schedules by asset freshness (chapter 30). Serving is BI queries against marts, usually on a dedicated virtual warehouse so dashboard users do not compete with transformation jobs.

Reverse ETL creates a dependency in the opposite direction: a sales team's CRM workflow now breaks if a dbt model changes a column. Treat models that feed reverse ETL as published interfaces with contracts and tests (chapter 33), not as internal tables.

Ten tools, each with its own lineage and access control; nobody sees the whole picture

blocks.text: **Costs at scale** come from three meters. Connector vendors often price on rows changed or synced per month (Fivetran uses 'monthly active rows'; check current pricing models), so a source that rewrites a status field on every row nightly can multiply the bill. Warehouse compute is billed per second of running virtual warehouses (chapter 29), and the main waste is full refreshes, oversized warehouses and dashboards that refresh every minute. BI and observability tools add per-seat or per-table fees. At a few terabytes the total is modest; at hundreds of terabytes with many sources, teams often find that ingestion plus compute exceeds what a self-managed lakehouse would cost, and start moving the heaviest workloads.

**Vendor sprawl** is the organisational cost. Each tool is reasonable on its own, but ten of them mean ten security reviews, ten places for credentials, overlapping lineage graphs and unclear ownership when something breaks between two of them.
41.7 When to choose it / when not

items: **Choose it** for analytics on structured data from SaaS tools and operational databases, with hourly-to-daily freshness.
**Choose it** when the team is small, SQL-strong, and should spend its time on modelling rather than infrastructure.
**Avoid it** as the only platform when volumes reach hundreds of terabytes of events or logs with heavy transformation; consider a lakehouse for that part.
**Avoid it** for sub-second or streaming use cases (chapters 40, 45, 46).
**Avoid it** when several engines (Spark ML, Trino, Snowflake) must share one copy of data; use Iceberg tables as the storage layer.
**Control it** with a cost dashboard per tool, a connector review before adding sources, and a single semantic layer instead of metrics in every BI tool.

blocks.title: A B2B SaaS company grows out of its first stack
blocks.text: A 200-person SaaS company built its platform in six weeks: Fivetran from Salesforce, Stripe, Zendesk and the production Postgres database into Snowflake, dbt Cloud for modelling, Looker for BI and Hightouch to send product-usage scores to Salesforce. Three years later, product event volume reached 2 billion rows a month and the platform cost had grown roughly fivefold.
items: The Postgres connector was the largest line: an `updated_at` touched by a nightly job made every row 'active'. Fixing the job cut the connector bill by about half.
Product events moved from Segment-to-Snowflake loading to Iceberg tables written by Spark, queried from Snowflake as Iceberg tables registered through an external catalog (see chapter 28).
A dozen full-refresh dbt models became incremental; the transformation warehouse was downsized one step.
Metric definitions in Looker and in a second BI tool were consolidated into one semantic layer.

blocks.title: Design and cost an MDS for a marketplace
blocks.text: A two-sided marketplace has a Postgres OLTP database (80 tables, 500 GB), Stripe, HubSpot and a mobile app emitting 30 million events per day. Leadership wants daily revenue and supply-demand dashboards, and the growth team wants churn-risk scores pushed into HubSpot. Design the stack layer by layer, the dbt layering, the orchestration between syncs and dbt, and the cost controls you would put in place from day one. State which data, if any, you would keep outside Snowflake and why.
hints: Which source drives the connector bill, and how could you reduce changed rows?
Separate warehouses for loading, transforming and BI.
Which model feeds HubSpot, and what contract protects it?

items: The MDS is managed ELT into a cloud warehouse, dbt for in-warehouse transformation, then BI, a semantic layer and reverse ETL.
It won on speed of delivery, elastic compute and software engineering practice for SQL.
dbt's sources, staging, intermediate and marts map directly onto bronze, silver and gold.
Cost grows across several usage-based meters: changed rows in connectors, warehouse compute seconds, per-seat tools.
Vendor sprawl and duplicated metric definitions are the main organisational failure modes.

blocks.q: What is the key difference between ELT in the MDS and ETL in the classic EDW?
options: ELT does not transform data at all
ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse with its elastic compute
ELT only works with NoSQL sources
blocks.explain: ELT moves transformation into the warehouse after loading. It still transforms and still uses dimensional models; the change is where and when the work happens.

blocks.q: A Fivetran bill doubles although the number of orders is flat. What is the most likely cause?
options: dbt tests are running more often
A source process now updates many existing rows, increasing changed (active) rows per month
Looker dashboards are refreshing more frequently
blocks.explain: Row-change-based connector pricing reacts to updates, not just inserts. dbt and Looker affect warehouse compute, not the connector bill.

blocks.q: Why should a dbt model that feeds reverse ETL be treated as a published interface?
options: Reverse ETL requires the model to be stored as Iceberg
Reverse ETL tools cannot read views
dbt cannot build incremental models used by reverse ETL
Operational tools such as the CRM depend on its columns and semantics, so changes can break business processes
blocks.explain: Reverse ETL makes downstream operational workflows depend on the model. The other options are technical claims that are not true.

blocks.q: Which situation most clearly signals that part of an MDS workload should move to an open lakehouse?
options: Hundreds of terabytes of event data must be shared by Spark ML, Trino and Snowflake without copies
A new SaaS source must be connected
The team wants to add a second dashboard
blocks.explain: Multi-engine access to very large data is where open table formats beat a single warehouse's internal storage. Adding a source or dashboard is the MDS's sweet spot.
